title: Game
prompt: I want to make a game
summary: A game is a system of parts that lets a player act, see the result and choose again. Its genre and device change the surface, while loops, resources, progression and balance remain underneath. The designer turns those parts into a core loop, tests the resulting experience and iterates. This view starts at a game being played on a screen and opens down to rules and measures.

nodes.plain: The finished game as a player meets it: a changing scene on a screen, with actions, rules and feedback underneath.
nodes.ask: What does the player see, do and learn in the next minute?

nodes.ask: Have we named every part that carries a state, rule or decision?

nodes.does: Keeps scope, omissions and balance comparisons visible as content expands.
nodes.ask: Can a new part be compared with the existing rows?

nodes.plain: The core loop is the chain of goal, choice, action, result and changed state that the player repeats during play.
nodes.does: Defines the game's immediate rhythm and the decisions players spend most of their time making.
nodes.ask: What does the player do again and again, and why does the next repetition matter?

feel.why: A warm moving ring makes the repeated cycle feel learnable but alive.

aka: what the player is trying to change
nodes.plain: A goal state is a desired condition that gives the next decision a direction.
nodes.does: Turns available actions into purposeful choices.
nodes.ask: What state would count as progress or success here?

nodes.plain: A choice point is a state in which two or more actions have different consequences worth weighing.
nodes.does: Creates agency and makes the core loop more than a sequence of button presses.
nodes.ask: What can the player choose, and what trade-off does each option carry?

nodes.plain: The game resolves the chosen action against current rules, parts and resources.
nodes.does: Converts intention into a causal result.
nodes.ask: What interactions happen between commitment and result?

nodes.plain: The game exposes the resolved result through changes in the scene, readouts, sounds or other signals.
nodes.does: Lets the player learn the relationship between action and outcome.
nodes.ask: What evidence arrives before the next choice?

nodes.plain: The updated values and positions after the action become the starting point for the next repetition.
nodes.does: Makes progress, danger and new choices accumulate.
nodes.ask: What is now different, and does that difference create a new decision?

nodes.does: Turns repeated actions into growth, pressure, scarcity and counterplay.
nodes.ask: Which resource flows amplify, brake or constrain the core loop?

nodes.plain: This game's boosting engine turns some resource now into greater future capacity or flow.
nodes.does: Creates reinforcing growth while asking the player to delay an immediate benefit.
nodes.ask: What can be invested now, and when does its larger flow arrive?

aka: pay now for a bigger engine
nodes.plain: A player chooses how much current resource to invest and how much future capacity that purchase creates.
nodes.does: Sets the strength and delay of the boosting engine.
nodes.ask: What is the payback time, and what immediate option is given up?
nodes.range: current resource spent; future flow gained

aka: a loop that slows or stops growth
nodes.plain: This game's braking engine drains a resource or reduces its future rate so another loop does not run away.
nodes.does: Regulates growth and can bring activity to a halt if its drain is too strong.
nodes.ask: What pressure consumes the resource, and when does it become too strong?

nodes.plain: A drain removes resource, and a stop threshold decides when the loop can no longer continue.
nodes.does: Sets the regulating force and the point at which activity stalls.
nodes.ask: How much drain preserves choice without making the loop inert?
nodes.range: drain per cycle; minimum viable resource

nodes.plain: This game's economy generates, destroys, trades or converts resources into value or capability.
nodes.does: Creates choices about where scarce resources go and tends to reinforce value through exchange.
nodes.ask: Which resource is created, spent, traded or converted, and for what gain?

nodes.plain: The economy specifies how resources enter play, leave play and change into other resources or capabilities.
nodes.does: Defines scarcity, opportunity cost and the timing of investment.
nodes.ask: What is the source, sink, exchange rate and delay?

nodes.plain: This game's ecology is a set of parts whose resource exchanges constrain or counterbalance one another.
nodes.does: Preserves dynamic tension by preventing one subsystem from making every other choice irrelevant.
nodes.ask: Which parts limit, counter or depend on one another?

nodes.plain: Competing parts use, deny or constrain the same opportunities, spaces or resources.
nodes.does: Creates counterplay and prevents a single subsystem from dominating every situation.
nodes.ask: What does each part make harder for the others?

nodes.plain: A reinforcing loop makes an increase feed the next increase, so capability or reward can snowball.
nodes.does: Creates momentum, investment pressure and the risk of runaway advantage.
nodes.ask: What grows, and what does that growth make easier next time?

feel.why: A rising spiral feels exciting because each turn widens the next one.

nodes.plain: The reward for a successful action increases the resources or options available for the next action.
nodes.does: Sets how strongly success compounds.
nodes.ask: Does this reward create useful momentum or remove future choices?

nodes.plain: Capability growth is the measured increase in actions, reach, output or resilience that a loop produces.
nodes.does: Shows whether the reinforcing loop is actually changing the player's available power.
nodes.ask: What new option or output exists after the investment?

nodes.plain: A balancing loop counters a change so the system settles, stabilises or stays within a useful range.
nodes.does: Protects decisions from runaway growth, dead ends and unbounded inflation.
nodes.ask: What signal rises, and what response reduces it?

feel.why: A cool weighted ring closes around a pressure and settles without going limp.

nodes.plain: A pressure raises a cost, threat or scarcity signal; a countermeasure reduces its effect or changes the available choice.
nodes.does: Converts imbalance into a new decision instead of an automatic win.
nodes.ask: What response can the player recognise and choose?

aka: a live balance, not a dead stop
nodes.plain: A settled range is the observed band in which the balancing loop still leaves meaningful choices.
nodes.does: Shows whether regulation preserves play rather than removing the variable entirely.
nodes.ask: Where does the system settle, and are decisions still alive there?
nodes.range: target band rather than one fixed value

nodes.plain: Progression changes what the player can do, understand or afford as play continues.
nodes.does: Paces new capability and complexity against the player's growing mental model.
nodes.ask: What changes, at which pace, and why is the next step worth reaching?

nodes.plain: A progression curve maps a measure such as level or time to cumulative capability, experience or cost.
nodes.does: Controls early accessibility, late-game distance and the rhythm of new understanding.
nodes.ask: Should growth be steady, accelerating, bounded or deliberately uneven?

feel.why: A rising ribbon can bend from gentle beginnings to sharp acceleration without losing its path.

items.name: Linear
items.plain: Each level adds the same amount: E(n)=100(n−1).

items.name: Polynomial
items.plain: A power such as E(n)=10(n−1)^2 makes later steps grow faster than early steps.

sources.label: Bulbapedia, Experience
sources.flag: polynomial experience curves and shipped formulas opened

items.name: Exponential
items.plain: E(n)=2^(n−1)−1 doubles the increment repeatedly, so late growth quickly dominates.

items.name: Logistic / S-curve

items.name: Subtract
items.plain: Damage = max(0, raw damage − armour); a high armour value can reach immunity.

sources.label: Armour investigation receipt
sources.flag: subtractive model shown as the comparison baseline; local receipt supplies the historical game case

items.name: Divide / ratio (League of Legends)
items.plain: Damage taken = raw × 100/(100 + armour), so armour reduces damage without reaching zero.

items.name: Divide / ratio (Warcraft III)
items.plain: Damage taken = raw/(1 + 0.06 × armour), equivalent to raw × 16.6667/(16.6667 + armour).

sources.label: Blizzard, Warcraft III Armor and Weapon Types

items.name: Percentage
items.plain: Damage taken = raw × max(0, 1 − 0.02 × armour); the 2% per point rate is an illustrative setting, not a universal rule.

sources.label: League of Legends Wiki, Armor
sources.flag: percentage mitigation framing opened; illustrative rate stated explicitly

items.name: Threshold
items.plain: Damage is 100% below armour 20 and 0% at or above armour 20; this is a hard breakpoint model.

items.plain: C(P)=P: each extra power point has the same cost.

aka: what the game feels like to play
nodes.plain: Player experience is the felt result of mechanics, dynamics, information, pacing and presentation as a person plays.
nodes.does: Gives every lower-level design choice a target beyond feature completion.
nodes.ask: What should the player feel, understand and want to do next?

feel.why: A warm, buoyant pulse represents an experience that is sensed rather than held.

aka: what the player thinks the system is
nodes.plain: The player's mental model is their working explanation of parts, rules, signals and likely outcomes.
nodes.does: Lets the player predict, plan and make choices without seeing the implementation.
nodes.ask: What does the player believe will happen before they commit?

feel.why: A smooth drifting form suggests an internal model that changes as evidence arrives.

nodes.plain: MDA links designed mechanics to run-time dynamics and then to the aesthetic experience the player feels.
nodes.does: Provides a shared lens for moving between rules, behaviour and experience during design and tuning.
nodes.ask: Which mechanic creates which dynamic, and which experience is that dynamic meant to support?

feel.why: Three linked lobes make the translation between design and experience visible.

nodes.plain: Mechanics are the particular rules, data and actions the game affords.
nodes.does: Supply the designed components from which dynamics arise.
nodes.ask: What rule or control is the player actually given?

nodes.plain: Dynamics are the run-time behaviours produced by mechanics acting on player inputs and one another over time.
nodes.does: Explains the patterns of play that emerge from the rules in motion.
nodes.ask: What pattern will these mechanics produce after several cycles?

feel.why: A restless flowing body captures motion that is caused by rules but not fully scripted.

nodes.plain: Aesthetics are the emotional responses and kinds of fun the game aims to evoke through play.
nodes.does: Sets the experience target against which mechanics and dynamics can be judged.
nodes.ask: Which specific feeling should this system support?

feel.why: A soft warm pulse represents a felt response rather than a visible object.

nodes.plain: A felt experience target names the specific response the game is trying to create, rather than calling every outcome simply fun.
nodes.does: Gives playtests a question sharper than whether the game is enjoyable in the abstract.
nodes.ask: What should a player feel at the end of this loop?

feel.why: A gentle pulse with a little energy fits a feeling that can intensify and release.

nodes.plain: The designer's loop sets an intended experience, puts a playable version in front of people, observes the gap and iterates.
nodes.does: Reduces the distance between the designed experience and the one players actually have.
nodes.ask: What did players actually experience, and what one change should we test next?

feel.why: A warm loop with a rough grain suggests repeated craft, evidence and correction.

aka: the experience we mean to make
nodes.plain: Design intent states the target experience, audience and important decisions before implementation details take over.
nodes.does: Gives observation a reference point for judging whether the system is working.
nodes.ask: What experience and decision are we deliberately trying to create?

feel.why: A light, warm point rises as a clear intention before it becomes a system.

nodes.plain: The target experience is a short, testable statement of what the player should feel, understand or choose.
nodes.does: Keeps iteration anchored to a human outcome rather than a list of features.
nodes.ask: What would we see a player do if the target were achieved?

feel.why: A soft amber pulse gives an abstract target a felt centre.

aka: put it in front of players
nodes.plain: A playtest puts a playable build in front of people and captures what they do, say and feel.
nodes.does: Supplies evidence about actual dynamics rather than imagined behaviour.
nodes.ask: What can players do without our explanation, and where do they diverge?

nodes.plain: An internal investment increases the future flow of the same resource. The player trades action now for greater future capacity.
nodes.ask: What internal investment increases the later flow?

feel.why: A buoyant spiral carries investment upwards into future capacity.

nodes.plain: A loop reduces a resource, sometimes also reducing its future rate or frequency of gain. It regulates another loop and can halt it if too strong.
nodes.ask: What drain regulates the other loop?

feel.why: A cool, heavy form presses down on runaway motion.

nodes.plain: Resources are exchanged or converted, producing a gain in value or capability. The pattern is predominantly reinforcing overall.
nodes.ask: Which resources exchange or convert into value?

feel.why: Warm rounded tokens circulate through exchanges and conversions.

nodes.plain: Resources are exchanged so parts constrain or counterbalance one another. The pattern is predominantly balancing, with reinforcing subsystems possible inside it.
nodes.ask: Which parts constrain one another through resource exchange?

feel.why: A textured cloud gives many interdependent parts room to move and push back.

assembly.title: List the parts
assembly.text: Name tokens, rules, attributes and behaviours, then keep them in a parts register.

assembly.title: Make the core loop
assembly.text: Join goal, choice, action resolution, feedback and the changed state into the repeatable play cycle.

assembly.title: Add engines, economy and ecology
assembly.text: Layer investment, brakes, resource exchanges and counter-pressure over the core loop.

assembly.title: Shape progression
assembly.text: Choose a curve, place gates and add capabilities at moments the player can understand.

assembly.title: Balance interactions
assembly.text: Choose interaction formulas, compare costs and counters, then measure hits-to-kill and time-to-kill.

assembly.title: Aim at an experience
assembly.text: Connect mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics to the player's mental model and felt target.

assembly.title: Close the designer loop
assembly.text: State intent, playtest, observe the gap and iterate one change at a time.

assembly.title: Put the system on screen
assembly.text: Render state and feedback in a readable layout on the selected device.

assembly.title: Ship the whole game
assembly.text: Join what the player sees and does to the parts, loops, systems, progression, balance, experience and designer practice.
